lessons.clue: It gives every webpage its structure.
lessons.definition: HTML is the structure and content of a page — headings, paragraphs, buttons, images, and links.
lessons.example: A button or a page heading starts as HTML.
lessons.readAloud: Read it like this: opening button tag, Save, closing button tag.

lessons.clue: It makes the page look and feel like itself.
lessons.definition: CSS controls the visual style: colors, spacing, layout, fonts, and tiny animations.
lessons.example: Making a button bright blue with soft corners is CSS.
lessons.readAloud: Read it like this: button, open brace, color blue, close brace.

lessons.clue: It reacts when someone clicks, types, or scrolls.
lessons.definition: JavaScript is code that makes a page respond and change when people interact with it.
lessons.example: A menu opening after a click is JavaScript at work.
lessons.readAloud: Read it like this: open menu, open parenthesis, close parenthesis.

lessons.clue: A live map of the page in the browser.
lessons.definition: The DOM is how a browser represents page elements so JavaScript can read or change them.
lessons.readAloud: Read it like this: document dot query selector, h one.

lessons.clue: The part of an app people can actually see and use.
lessons.definition: Front-end development builds the screens, interactions, and experiences that run in a browser.
lessons.example: The login form, product photos, and checkout button are front-end.
lessons.readAloud: Read it like this: show login form, open parenthesis, close parenthesis.

lessons.clue: It listens for requests and sends useful answers back.
lessons.definition: A server is a computer or cloud service that runs back-end code for an app.
lessons.example: After you log in, a server can check whether your account exists.
lessons.readAloud: Read it like this: app dot get, profile, get profile.

lessons.clue: A tidy place for an app to remember things.
lessons.definition: A database stores organized information such as user accounts, posts, orders, or scores.
lessons.example: Your saved profile details can live in a database.
lessons.readAloud: Read it like this: select star from users.

lessons.clue: A clear doorway for software to ask for information.
lessons.definition: An API is an agreed way for different parts of software to request and share information.
lessons.example: The front-end can ask an API for a list of your saved tasks.
lessons.readAloud: Read it like this: fetch, API tasks.

lessons.clue: The check that answers: “Are you really you?”
lessons.definition: Authentication verifies someone’s identity before an app lets them access protected information.
lessons.example: Checking a password securely happens on the back-end.
lessons.readAloud: Read it like this: if is valid, log in.

lessons.clue: The behind-the-scenes logic that powers the screen.
lessons.definition: Back-end development handles data, business rules, security, and requests away from the visible page.
lessons.example: Calculating a total and saving an order are back-end jobs.
lessons.readAloud: Read it like this: save order, order.

lessons.clue: One part asks. Another part answers.
lessons.definition: A request asks for something; a response is the information or result sent back.
lessons.example: Your browser requests your profile, and the server responds with it.
lessons.readAloud: Read it like this: fetch, API profile.

lessons.clue: It joins the visible experience and the system behind it.
lessons.definition: Full-stack work spans both front-end and back-end, helping a feature travel from screen to data and back.
lessons.example: A full-stack developer might build a form and the API that saves it.
lessons.readAloud: Read it like this: send form to API.

lessons.clue: A fake message or site that tries to trick you.
lessons.definition: Phishing uses believable messages, links, or websites to steal information such as passwords or payment details.

lessons.clue: Software made to harm, spy, or break in.
lessons.definition: Malware is malicious software designed to disrupt a device, steal data, or gain unwanted access.

lessons.clue: Malware that locks data and demands money.
lessons.definition: Ransomware can encrypt or block access to files, then demand payment for their return.

lessons.clue: A weakness someone could take advantage of.
lessons.definition: A vulnerability is a flaw in software, settings, or a process that could be exploited.

lessons.clue: A repair that strengthens software.
lessons.definition: A patch or update changes software to fix known problems, including security vulnerabilities.

lessons.clue: More than one way to prove it is you.
lessons.definition: Multi-factor authentication asks for an extra sign-in factor, such as an authenticator code, in addition to a password.

lessons.clue: The identity check at sign-in.
lessons.definition: Authentication verifies who someone is before an account or system lets them in.

lessons.clue: The permission check after sign-in.
lessons.definition: Authorization decides what an authenticated person is allowed to view, change, or use.

lessons.clue: Only the access needed for the job.
lessons.definition: Least privilege gives a person or system the minimum permissions needed, limiting the impact of mistakes or misuse.

lessons.clue: Turning data into protected unreadable form.
lessons.definition: Encryption transforms readable data into protected data that should only be understandable with the right key.

lessons.clue: A separate copy for recovery.
lessons.definition: Backups are copies of important data kept so it can be restored after loss, damage, or a ransomware incident.

lessons.clue: When unsafe input can change a database request.
lessons.definition: SQL injection is a risk when untrusted input is treated as database-query instructions; parameterized queries help keep data separate from commands.

lessons.clue: What does = do?
lessons.definition: Bind a name to a value. Use == to compare.

lessons.clue: How do you name a score?
lessons.definition: Use descriptive snake_case. Names are case-sensitive; avoid keywords and leading digits.

lessons.clue: Do you import print?
lessons.definition: No. Built-ins are available without imports. Avoid naming your variables print or len.

lessons.clue: What does len count?
lessons.definition: For a list, len counts items; for a simple string, characters.

lessons.clue: How can you inspect a value?
lessons.definition: type reveals its type. Quoted digits are text, not numbers.

lessons.clue: Does input return a number?
lessons.definition: input returns text. Convert numeric input before arithmetic.

lessons.clue: Can int parse decimal text?
lessons.definition: int("6.8") raises ValueError. Parse with float first if truncation is intended.

lessons.clue: Does int round decimals?
lessons.definition: No: conversion truncates toward zero. Python has int, float, and complex numbers.

lessons.clue: How do you join text and a number?
lessons.definition: Convert the number with str, or use an f-string.

lessons.clue: How is a list different from a dictionary?
lessons.definition: A list holds a sequence; a dictionary maps keys to values.

lessons.clue: Can one line assign two names?
lessons.definition: Yes. Match the number of names and values.

lessons.clue: How do you total a collection?
lessons.definition: sum adds numeric items. min and max find extremes; sorted makes a sorted list.

questions.question: Which part of a web app do people see, tap, and type into?
questions.explanation: Exactly — the front-end is the visible, interactive experience.

questions.question: Which language gives a webpage its structure, such as headings, paragraphs, links, and buttons?
questions.explanation: HTML provides the meaningful building blocks and content of a webpage.

questions.question: A page already has a button, but it needs a blue background, rounded corners, and more space around it. What should you use?
questions.explanation: CSS controls how page elements look and are arranged: color, spacing, typography, and layout.

questions.question: Which language is a good fit for opening a menu after someone clicks its icon?
questions.explanation: JavaScript adds behavior, including responding to clicks, typing, scrolling, and other events.

questions.question: In the browser, what is the DOM?
choices: A cloud service for storing files
A live representation of page elements JavaScript can read or change
questions.explanation: The DOM is the browser’s live map of the page, so JavaScript can find, update, add, or remove elements.

questions.question: Where should an app safely check a password and load private account data?
questions.explanation: Sensitive checks and data work belong on the back-end, away from code every browser visitor can inspect.

questions.question: What is a server’s main job in a typical web app?
choices: Listen for requests, run back-end logic, and send responses
questions.explanation: A server receives requests, does useful work such as checking rules or data, and returns a response.

questions.question: Which item is a good fit for a database?
choices: The color of one heading while it is loading
questions.explanation: Databases store organized information an app needs to remember, such as accounts, tasks, posts, or orders.

questions.question: What does an API give different parts of software?
choices: A shared, agreed way to request and exchange data
A way to make passwords visible
questions.explanation: An API is a clear contract for how one part of software can ask another part for information or an action.

questions.question: What question does authentication answer?
choices: “Are you really who you say you are?”
questions.explanation: Authentication verifies identity, such as when an app checks sign-in credentials.

questions.question: A browser sends “please give me my saved tasks” to an API. That outgoing message is a…
questions.explanation: A request asks for something. The API or server then sends a response with a result, data, or an error.

questions.question: A developer builds a checkout screen, an API route to receive the order, and database code to save it. What kind of work is this?
questions.explanation: Full-stack work spans the visible experience and the systems behind it, connecting a feature end to end.

questions.question: Which sequence best describes saving a new task from a web page?
choices: Browser sends a request → server validates it → database saves it → server sends a response
CSS sends a request → DOM saves it → browser restarts
questions.explanation: A common full-stack flow starts in the browser, travels through a server to data storage, then returns a result.

questions.question: A person submits a new comment. Which HTTP-style action most closely matches creating that new item?
questions.explanation: POST is commonly used when sending data to create a new resource, such as a comment or account.

questions.question: After someone signs in, an app checks whether they may edit a team’s billing details. What is that permission check called?
questions.explanation: Authentication establishes who someone is; authorization determines what that signed-in person is allowed to do.

questions.question: A layout looks great on a laptop but its cards overflow on a phone. What is the best next step?
choices: Add responsive CSS for smaller screens
Move the cards into a database
Store the phone in a server
questions.explanation: Responsive CSS, often with flexible layouts or media queries, lets an interface adapt to different screen sizes.

questions.question: Which choice makes a sign-up form more accessible to people using a screen reader?
choices: Use placeholder text instead of labels
Use only color to explain errors
Give every input a clear visible label
questions.explanation: Clear labels help everyone understand each field and give assistive technology a reliable name for it.

questions.question: A custom clickable card should also work for someone navigating with a keyboard. What is the strongest starting choice?
choices: Use a plain div and only mouse clicks
Make it a semantic button when it performs an action
questions.explanation: A real button brings helpful keyboard behavior and accessibility information by default.

questions.question: Your task list fails to load. What is a useful first debugging move?
choices: Change every color in the app
Check the browser console and Network panel for errors or failed requests
Ignore the issue and refresh forever
questions.explanation: The console and Network panel can reveal JavaScript errors, failed API calls, response details, and other useful clues.

questions.question: An app builds a database query from untrusted text someone typed. Which approach is safer?
choices: Use parameterized queries and validate input
Paste the text directly into the query
Trust every input because it came from a form
questions.explanation: Parameterized queries keep data separate from query instructions, helping protect against injection attacks.

questions.question: Which prompt gives an AI agent the clearest request for a phone-friendly profile card?
choices: “Use CSS to make the profile card responsive below 600px, stack its content, and keep text readable.”
“Use the database to fix the screen.”
questions.explanation: A strong prompt names the tool, the goal, the context, and clear success criteria.

questions.question: Which prompt best asks an AI agent for an accessible sign-up form?
choices: “Use only placeholders so the form is cleaner.”
“Build semantic HTML with visible labels, an email field, and clear error feedback.”
questions.explanation: Naming semantic HTML, labels, fields, and feedback gives the agent useful accessibility requirements.

questions.question: An AI agent suggests placing a private API key in front-end JavaScript. What is the right response?
choices: Ask it to move the secret to protected server-side configuration
Leave it there because the code is minified
Put the key in a CSS comment
Show the key in the login form
questions.explanation: Anything sent to the browser can be inspected. Private keys and other secrets must stay on the server.

questions.question: Which prompt gives an AI agent the clearest API task?
choices: “Create a POST /api/tasks endpoint that validates a title, saves the task, returns JSON on success, and explains validation errors.”
questions.explanation: A useful implementation prompt specifies the route, input, behavior, successful response, and failure behavior.

questions.question: An AI-generated task list is blank. Which follow-up prompt is most useful for debugging?
choices: “Check the browser console and Network request for the tasks API; explain any error, status code, and fix.”
questions.explanation: A focused debugging prompt gives the agent evidence to inspect and asks for an explanation plus a safe next step.

questions.question: What is phishing designed to do?
choices: Trick someone into sharing information or taking an unsafe action
Encrypt a trusted file for storage
questions.explanation: Phishing relies on deception — often a convincing message, link, or login page — to steal information or prompt an unsafe action.

questions.question: An unexpected email says your account will close today and asks you to sign in through its link. What is the safest first move?
choices: Open the service through a known app or typed address and check there
questions.explanation: Avoid using a surprising link. Reach the service through a trusted route and check whether the alert is real.

questions.question: Which description best fits malware?
choices: Software designed to harm, spy on, or gain unwanted access
A method for making a password longer
questions.explanation: Malware is malicious software. It can disrupt devices, steal information, or enable unwanted access.

questions.question: What is ransomware known for?
choices: Locking or encrypting data and demanding payment
questions.explanation: Ransomware commonly blocks access to data, then demands payment. Prepared backups can make recovery possible.

questions.question: What is a vulnerability?
choices: A weakness in software, settings, or a process that could be exploited
A backup copy of a database
questions.explanation: A vulnerability is a weakness that could be used to compromise a system, account, or data.

questions.question: Why do software patches and updates matter?
choices: They only change an app’s icon
They can fix known bugs and security vulnerabilities
questions.explanation: Updates often repair known issues, including security flaws. They reduce risk, though no single step eliminates all risk.

questions.question: What does MFA add to a sign-in?
choices: A second or additional proof of identity
questions.explanation: MFA asks for more than one factor, such as a password plus an authenticator approval or security key.

questions.question: A person enters a password and then approves a code in an authenticator app. What are they using?
questions.explanation: A password plus an authenticator approval is a common multi-factor authentication flow.

questions.question: Authentication answers which question?
choices: What color should the page be?
questions.explanation: Authentication verifies identity — for example, confirming that a sign-in belongs to the account holder.

questions.question: Authorization answers which question?
choices: Are you really this account holder?
What are you allowed to access or change?
Has the device installed an update?
questions.explanation: Authorization comes after identity is established and determines what that person is permitted to do.

questions.question: A teammate can view a report but cannot edit it. Which concept is controlling that difference?
questions.explanation: Authorization controls permissions, such as whether a signed-in person may view, edit, or administer something.

questions.question: What does least privilege mean?
choices: People receive only the access needed for their work
Passwords should be shared with a team
Every account should have the same role
questions.explanation: Least privilege limits access to what is needed, reducing the impact of mistakes, compromised accounts, or misuse.

questions.question: A new contractor only needs to read one project folder. Which permission choice best follows least privilege?
choices: Give access to every company folder
Give read-only access to that project folder
questions.explanation: The narrow, read-only permission meets the need without granting unrelated access.

questions.question: What does encryption do to data?
choices: Turns readable data into protected data that needs the right key to read
Removes the need for access controls
questions.explanation: Encryption protects confidentiality by transforming readable data into a protected form that requires the appropriate key.

questions.question: Which statement about encryption is most accurate?
choices: It replaces passwords, permissions, and updates
It is one protection that works alongside other security practices
It is only useful for photos
questions.explanation: Encryption is valuable, but security works in layers — it complements strong sign-ins, permissions, updates, and careful habits.

questions.question: Why are backups important in a ransomware situation?
choices: They can provide a separate copy for recovery
They make a suspicious link safe
questions.explanation: Separate, usable backups can help restore data after an incident instead of relying on the affected copy.

questions.question: Which is the best description of a useful backup?
choices: The only copy of a file on the same device
A separate copy that can be restored when needed
A password written in a chat
A file that everyone can change
questions.explanation: A backup should be a separate recoverable copy, and it is wise to check that restoration actually works.

questions.question: What creates the risk of SQL injection?
choices: Treating untrusted input as part of a database command
questions.explanation: SQL injection can happen when input is interpreted as query instructions instead of handled purely as data.

questions.question: Which approach helps reduce SQL injection risk?
choices: Build a query by pasting user input directly into it
Use parameterized queries and validate input
Hide the query in a CSS file
Trust input because it came from a form
questions.explanation: Parameterized queries keep data separate from query instructions, while validation limits unexpected input.

questions.question: You receive a chat message from a coworker asking for an urgent gift-card purchase. What is the safest next step?
choices: Act immediately because it sounds urgent
Verify the request through a known, separate channel
questions.explanation: Urgency is a common social-engineering tactic. Verify unusual requests using a trusted way to reach the person.

questions.question: An app alerts you to a sign-in you do not recognize. What is a sensible immediate response?
choices: Ignore it if the app still works
Change the password, review active sessions, and report it through the service
Share the alert online with your password
questions.explanation: Treat unexpected sign-in alerts seriously: secure the account, remove unknown sessions, and use the service’s official support path if needed.

questions.question: Which password habit is strongest?
choices: Use long, unique passwords stored in a reputable password manager
Share a password in a group chat
Use a short word plus your birth year
questions.explanation: Unique, long passwords limit damage from one compromised site. A password manager makes them practical to use.

questions.question: What is the main benefit of using different passwords for different accounts?
choices: It makes phishing messages more believable
One stolen password cannot unlock every account
It removes the need for MFA
It turns a vulnerability into a patch
questions.explanation: Unique passwords contain the fallout if one service experiences a breach or a password is exposed.

questions.question: Someone sends you an unexpected file and says, “Enable editing right away.” What is the safer choice?
choices: Verify the sender and purpose before opening or enabling anything
questions.explanation: Unexpected files and unusual instructions deserve a pause. Verify independently before opening or enabling content.

questions.question: Which response best combines authentication, authorization, and least privilege?
choices: Verify a person’s identity, then give only the permissions needed for their role
Let anyone edit everything after entering an email
Use the same administrator account for the whole team
Skip sign-in if the person knows the project name
questions.explanation: A safer system confirms identity, checks the role, and grants only the minimum access that role needs.
